New home prices in 70 Chinese cities fell -3.20% YoY in July, after a -3.30% YoY decline in June.

Only 17 of the 70 surveyed cities recorded price gains, with tier-1 cities flat on average, tier-2 cities declining -0.10% MoM, and tier-3 cities falling -0.30% MoM.

Meanwhile, existing home prices decreased -0.29% MoM in July, following a -0.32% decline in the prior month.

China's property prices have now declined continuously since mid-2023.

It's 2008 for China's housing market.

BREAKING: Foreign holdings of US Treasuries dropped -$72 billion in June, to $9.30 trillion, to the lowest level since January.

This marks the 3rd monthly decline over the last 4 months, totaling -$190 billion.

Japan, the largest foreign holder, reduced its holdings by -$26 billion in June, to $1.12 trillion, the lowest since January 2025.

The UK, the 2nd-largest holder, cut its holdings by -$9 billion, to $940 billion, the 2nd-largest on record.

China, the 3rd-largest holder, trimmed its holdings by -$26 billion, to $633 billion, the lowest since September 2008.

Meanwhile, foreign official holders, such as central banks and government entities, reduced their Treasury holdings by -$70 billion in June, to $3.78 trillion, the lowest since February 2024.

Foreign demand for US Treasuries is losing momentum.

The entire world wants US stocks.

Foreign investors outside the US purchased +$181.4 billion of US equities in June.

The private sector alone bought a record +$144.7 billion, bringing an annualized rate to +$1.74 trillion, an all-time high.

Over the past 3 months, private purchases have totaled +$351.1 billion, equivalent to an annualized pace of +$1.4 trillion, also an all-time high.

This surpasses the 2025 annualized record by ~$400.0 billion.

By comparison, foreign official institutions, such as central banks and sovereign wealth funds, purchased +$36.7 billion in June.

As a result, private investors accounted for ~80% of all foreign equity purchases over this period.

The appetite for US stocks is stronger than ever.

Cracks in the US private credit industry are widening:

Loans marked as non-accrual across the 20 largest publicly traded business development companies (BDCs) rose +0.8 percentage points in Q2 2026, to a median 2.8% of cost, the highest since 2017.

BDCs are publicly traded firms that lend to small, mid-sized, and distressed US businesses, giving retail investors access to private credit markets.

This increase means a growing share of private-credit borrowers have either stopped making payments or are at risk of defaulting on their loans.

Furthermore, new funding commitments minus the value of investments repaid or sold across the 12 largest listed BDCs fell to -$2.5 billion in Q2 2025, the lowest in at least 2.5 years.

This marks the 3rd consecutive quarter of negative net funding.

Meanwhile, Fitch Ratings said last week that private credit defaults rose to an all-time high in July.

Stress in the $2 trillion private credit market is intensifying.

US hiring is showing signs of a recovery:

20% of small business owners said in July that they plan to hire over the next 3 months, the highest since October 2022.

By comparison, the average since the 1970s is just ~11%.

This also marks a +9 percentage point MoM increase, the largest monthly improvement in hiring intentions on record.

This even surpasses the sharp recovery seen following the 2020 pandemic drop.

Historically, this indicator has led nonfarm private payrolls by 3-6 months, as small firms account for ~46% of all US private sector employment.

If history holds, a stronger jobs report could be just months away.
